sections.title: SOV Word Order
sections.rule: Japanese sentences put the verb at the very end: Subject + Object + Verb. The topic usually comes first, marked by は, and the object is marked by を. Modifiers always precede what they modify.
sections.example_target: 私はりんごを食べます。
sections.example_target_2: 彼は日本語を勉強します。
sections.example_ref: English: I eat an apple. / He studies Japanese.
sections.note: Romaji: Watashi wa ringo o tabemasu. The verb never floats to the middle — hunt for it at the end to decode any sentence.

sections.title: Topic は vs Subject が
sections.rule: は (wa) marks the topic — what the sentence is about, often already known. が (ga) marks the grammatical subject, introducing new information or singling one thing out exclusively.
sections.example_target: 私は学生です。
sections.example_target_2: 誰が来ましたか。
sections.example_ref: English: As for me, I'm a student. / Who came?
sections.note: Romaji: Watashi wa gakusei desu / Dare ga kimashita ka. Answers to 'who/what' questions take が, because they are the new focus.

sections.title: Core Particles を に で と
sections.rule: を marks the direct object; に marks a destination, a point in time, or the location where something exists; で marks where an action happens or the means used; と means 'together with' or 'and'.
sections.example_target: 友達と学校でお弁当を食べます。
sections.example_target_2: 三時に東京に行きます。
sections.example_ref: English: I eat a bento at school with a friend. / I go to Tokyo at three o'clock.
sections.note: Romaji: Tomodachi to gakkō de obentō o tabemasu. Remember に = existence/arrival point, で = active location.

sections.title: Verb Forms: dict, ます, て, た
sections.rule: Every verb has a dictionary form (食べる), a polite ます form (食べます), a connective て form (食べて), and a plain past た form (食べた). する and 来る (くる) are the two irregulars.
sections.example_target: 毎日ご飯を食べて、テレビを見ます。
sections.example_target_2: 昨日、宿題をしました。
sections.example_ref: English: Every day I eat and watch TV. / Yesterday I did my homework.
sections.note: Romaji: Mainichi gohan o tabete, terebi o mimasu. Master the て form early — it links clauses and builds dozens of grammar patterns.

sections.title: い-adj vs な-adjectives
sections.rule: い-adjectives conjugate themselves: 暑い → 暑くない (not hot) → 暑かった (was hot). な-adjectives behave like nouns, using じゃない and でした, and take な before a noun (静かな部屋).
sections.example_target: この部屋は静かですが、暑いです。
sections.example_target_2: 昨日は寒くなかったです。
sections.example_ref: English: This room is quiet but hot. / Yesterday wasn't cold.
sections.note: Romaji: Kono heya wa shizuka desu ga, atsui desu. いい (good) is irregular: よくない, よかった — never いくない.

sections.title: て-form + います
sections.rule: て form + います expresses an action in progress (食べています = is eating). With certain verbs it instead describes a resulting state (住んでいます = lives, 結婚しています = is married).
sections.example_target: 今、母は電話で話しています。
sections.example_target_2: 私は大阪に住んでいます。
sections.example_ref: English: Right now my mother is talking on the phone. / I live in Osaka.
sections.note: Romaji: Ima, haha wa denwa de hanashite imasu. 知っています means 'I know' (a state); its negative is 知りません, not 知っていません.

sections.title: Politeness: ます/です vs Plain
sections.rule: The ます/です style is the polite default for strangers, teachers, and work. The plain (dictionary) style is casual, used with close friends and family, and is also required inside relative clauses.
sections.example_target: 明日、映画を見に行きますか。
sections.example_target_2: うん、一緒に行こう。
sections.example_ref: English: Are you going to see a movie tomorrow? / Yeah, let's go together.
sections.note: Romaji: Ashita, eiga o mi ni ikimasu ka. When unsure, choose the polite form — over-politeness is safe, under-politeness offends.

sections.title: Counters and Classifiers
sections.rule: Japanese counts things with number + classifier chosen by shape or type: 〜つ (general), 〜人 (people), 〜枚 (flat), 〜本 (long), 〜匹 (small animals). Several trigger sound changes (一本 ippon, 三匹 sanbiki).
sections.example_target: りんごを三つとビールを二本ください。
sections.example_target_2: 教室に学生が五人います。
sections.example_ref: English: Three apples and two beers, please. / There are five students in the classroom.
sections.note: Romaji: Ringo o mittsu to bīru o nihon kudasai. The generic 〜つ (ひとつ, ふたつ, みっつ) rescues you when you forget the specific counter.

sections.title: Desire: たい and たがる
sections.rule: Add たい to the verb stem for your own wish: 食べたい (I want to eat). たい conjugates like an い-adjective (食べたくない, 食べたかった). For a third person's desire, use 〜たがる or 〜たがっている.
sections.example_target: 冷たい水が飲みたいです。
sections.example_target_2: 弟は新しいゲームを買いたがっています。
sections.example_ref: English: I want to drink cold water. / My little brother wants to buy a new game.
sections.note: Romaji: Tsumetai mizu ga nomitai desu. The object of たい often takes が instead of を — both are heard, but が is more traditional.

sections.title: Four Conditionals: と ば たら なら
sections.rule: と = automatic/natural result (押すと開く). ば = general hypothesis (行けば). たら = the most versatile 'if/when', good for one-time future events (食べたら). なら = 'if it's the case that' (行くなら).
sections.example_target: 駅に着いたら、電話してください。
sections.example_target_2: 日本に行くなら、京都がおすすめです。
sections.example_ref: English: When you arrive at the station, please call. / If you're going to Japan, I recommend Kyoto.
sections.note: Romaji: Eki ni tsuitara, denwa shite kudasai. Default to たら when unsure — it covers the widest range of 'if/when' meanings.

sections.title: Giving and Receiving
sections.rule: あげる = give outward (I/we to others), くれる = give inward (others to me/my side), もらう = receive. Adding these to a て-form verb expresses doing or receiving a favor.
sections.example_target: 友達が宿題を手伝ってくれました。
sections.example_target_2: 母に誕生日プレゼントをもらいました。
sections.example_ref: English: My friend helped me with my homework. / I received a birthday present from my mother.
sections.note: Romaji: Tomodachi ga shukudai o tetsudatte kuremashita. くれる always points toward the speaker — you can never くれる to someone else.

sections.title: Potential Form: Can Do
sections.rule: To say 'can do', ichidan verbs replace る with られる (食べる→食べられる), godan verbs shift the final -u to -e + る (行く→行ける, 飲む→飲める). する→できる, 来る→来られる.
sections.example_target: 私は漢字が少し読めます。
sections.example_target_2: ここでは日本語が話せます。
sections.example_ref: English: I can read kanji a little. / Here you can speak Japanese.
sections.note: Romaji: Watashi wa kanji ga sukoshi yomemasu. The object of a potential verb usually switches from を to が (漢字が読める).

sections.title: Volitional: Let's / I'll
sections.rule: The volitional expresses 'let's' or intention: polite 〜ましょう (行きましょう), plain 〜よう / 〜おう (食べよう, 行こう). 〜ましょうか offers to do something for someone.
sections.example_target: 疲れたから、少し休みましょう。
sections.example_target_2: 荷物を持ちましょうか。
sections.example_ref: English: We're tired, so let's rest a bit. / Shall I carry your bag?
sections.note: Romaji: Tsukareta kara, sukoshi yasumimashō. 〜(よ)うと思う ('I think I'll…') is a soft, natural way to announce your own plans.

sections.title: Permission and Prohibition
sections.rule: て-form + もいい(です) grants permission ('may'). て-form + はいけない / はだめ forbids ('must not'). Raise politeness with ですか for asking and 〜ません for a firm no.
sections.example_target: ここに座ってもいいですか。
sections.example_target_2: 美術館で写真を撮ってはいけません。
sections.example_ref: English: May I sit here? / You must not take photos in the museum.
sections.note: Romaji: Koko ni suwatte mo ii desu ka. は in 〜てはいけない is pronounced 'wa'; casually it contracts to 〜ちゃだめ (撮っちゃだめ).

sections.title: Causative and Passive
sections.rule: Causative せる/させる means make or let someone do (食べさせる). Passive れる/られる means an action is done to you, often unpleasantly (褒められる, 盗まれる). Causative-passive expresses being forced to do (行かせられる).
sections.example_target: 先生は学生に漢字を書かせました。
sections.example_target_2: 電車で足を踏まれました。
sections.example_ref: English: The teacher made the students write kanji. / My foot was stepped on in the train.
sections.note: Romaji: Sensei wa gakusei ni kanji o kakasemashita. The doer of a passive action is marked by に (先生に褒められた = praised by the teacher).

sections.title: Plain Casual Forms
sections.rule: Casual speech uses plain forms: negative ない (食べない), plain past た (行った), past negative なかった (食べなかった). These same plain forms are mandatory before nouns and inside subordinate clauses.
sections.example_target: 昨日は忙しくて、どこにも行かなかった。
sections.example_target_2: これは私が作った料理だよ。
sections.example_ref: English: I was busy yesterday and didn't go anywhere. / This is a dish I made.
sections.note: Romaji: Kinō wa isogashikute, doko ni mo ikanakatta. Even in polite speech, relative clauses use plain forms — 昨日買った本 (the book I bought yesterday).

sections.title: Obligation: Must Do
sections.rule: Obligation is built on the negative conditional: 〜なければなりません / 〜なければいけません ('must'). Casual contractions are 〜なきゃ and 〜ないと. The literal meaning is 'if you don't, it won't do'.
sections.example_target: 明日は早く起きなければなりません。
sections.example_target_2: もう行かなきゃ。
sections.example_ref: English: I have to get up early tomorrow. / I've gotta go now.
sections.note: Romaji: Ashita wa hayaku okinakereba narimasen. 〜なくてもいいです is the opposite — 'you don't have to' (行かなくてもいいです).

sections.title: Giving Advice
sections.rule: 〜ほうがいい recommends an action; use the past た form for stronger advice (休んだほうがいい). 〜べき states what one ought to do as a principle. 〜ないほうがいい advises against.
sections.example_target: 熱があるなら、病院に行ったほうがいいですよ。
sections.example_target_2: 学生はもっと本を読むべきだ。
sections.example_ref: English: If you have a fever, you'd better go to the hospital. / Students should read more books.
sections.note: Romaji: Netsu ga aru nara, byōin ni itta hō ga ii desu yo. べき sounds moralistic and formal — for gentle suggestions, prefer 〜ほうがいい.

sections.title: Quotation with と
sections.rule: と marks a quote before 思う (think), 言う (say), or 聞く (hear). The clause before と stays in plain form. Direct quotes use 「」 with と言う.
sections.example_target: 明日は雨が降ると思います。
sections.example_target_2: 彼は「また来ます」と言いました。
sections.example_ref: English: I think it will rain tomorrow. / He said, "I'll come again."
sections.note: Romaji: Ashita wa ame ga furu to omoimasu. The clause before と思う is always plain form, even in otherwise polite speech.

sections.title: なる: To Become
sections.rule: なる expresses change of state. い-adjectives drop い and add く (寒くなる = get cold). な-adjectives and nouns take に (元気になる, 医者になる). The pattern shows natural, gradual change.
sections.example_target: 日本語がだんだん上手になりました。
sections.example_target_2: 春になると、桜が咲きます。
sections.example_ref: English: My Japanese gradually got better. / When spring comes, the cherry blossoms bloom.
sections.note: Romaji: Nihongo ga dandan jōzu ni narimashita. する = you cause the change; なる = the change happens on its own.

sections.title: Conjecture: でしょう and かもしれない
sections.rule: 〜でしょう / plain 〜だろう expresses a confident guess ('probably'). 〜かもしれません signals a weaker possibility ('might'). Both attach to plain forms; nouns and な-adjectives drop だ before them.
sections.example_target: 明日は晴れるでしょう。
sections.example_target_2: 電車が遅れているので、遅刻するかもしれません。
sections.example_ref: English: It will probably be sunny tomorrow. / The train is delayed, so I might be late.
sections.note: Romaji: Ashita wa hareru deshō. Spoken with rising intonation, 〜でしょう? seeks agreement ('right?') rather than stating a guess.

sections.title: Keigo: Honorific Speech
sections.rule: Business Japanese splits into 尊敬語 (sonkeigo, elevating the listener: いらっしゃる, なさる, 召し上がる) and 謙譲語 (kenjōgo, humbling yourself: 参る, いたす, 申す, いただく). A neutral polite layer, 丁寧語, uses です/ます.
sections.example_target: 社長はもうお帰りになりました。
sections.example_target_2: 私が資料をお持ちいたします。
sections.example_ref: English: The president has already gone home. / I will bring the documents.
sections.note: Romaji: Shachō wa mō okaeri ni narimashita. Golden rule: raise the other person with sonkeigo, lower yourself with kenjōgo — never mix them up.
